statement: Caching is covered now as setup for a discussion the teacher will trigger the next morning; questions follow afterwards.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We'll move to caching. Then after this, we'll again have a quick question.

statement: People misunderstand caching a lot: caching is not just in-memory caching.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Like people misunderstand caching a lot. So caching is not just in-memory caching.

statement: Caching is anything, literally anything, that helps you save a heavy computation or heavy operation so that you do not have to do it again.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Caching is anything, literally anything that helps you save a heavy computation.

statement: Memoization in dynamic programming is classic caching.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Dynamic programming, memoization is caching. Classic caching.

statement: Many people equate caches with RAM, but caches are not only RAM-based: disk can be used as a cache, and so can the network.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Caches are not only RAM based. You can use disk as a cache. You can use network as a cache.

statement: Whatever result you save so you can refer to it instead of redoing an expensive computation, expensive operation or expensive IO becomes a cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you can just basically refer to it to in order to not do that expensive computation, expensive operation, expensive IO.

statement: Caching typically helps reduce disk IO or network IO; the usual habit of caching in RAM comes from RAM being faster than disk, so the core idea there is saving expensive disk IO by keeping the computation in RAM.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what the core idea is, we are saving this expensive disk IO by caching the computation in RAM.

statement: If a network call is expensive, you can cache its result on the local disk and read from that disk instead of making the network call; that cache saves expensive network IO.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if you cache on the disk and you refer to that local disk rather than making that expensive network call?

statement: A cache is anything that saves one of three things: an expensive disk IO, an expensive network IO or an expensive computation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Anything which can help you save an expensive disk IO, expensive network IO or expensive computation. All three.

statement: Computer science has four things: disk, network, CPU and RAM.
detail: The teacher calls this something he always says; it frames which expensive operations a cache can save.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: computer science has four things. Disk, network, CPU, RAM.

statement: Be very creative in finding usages of caches.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So be very creative in finding usage of caches.

statement: Caches in general are just glorified key-value hash tables, nothing more.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So caches in general are just glorified hash tables, that's it. Key-value hash table, that's it, right?

statement: Redis offers a bunch of advanced data structures such as HyperLogLog, Bloom filters and geospatial queries, but underneath it is still hash tables and key-values.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you're using Redis, it has a bunch of advanced data structures like HyperLogLog, Bloom filters, geospatial queries and whatnot.

statement: In the blog example the cache is typically a remote cache that any API server can talk to; logically it sits between the database and the API servers.
case_study: Blog (multi-user blogging app) example: one remote cache shared by all API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we typically have a remote cache that can be communicated that any API server can talk to.

statement: Standard cache read flow: the request reaches an API server, which first checks the cache; if the data is there it returns it; if not, it reads from the database, puts the data into the cache and returns it to the user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: API server first checks the cache, if it has the data it returns it back.

statement: A remote cache ensures that no matter which API server a request goes to, all of them read from the same cache: there is just one copy of the data in the cache and everyone reads it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Having a remote cache helps us ensure that no matter where the request goes, they all go to the same cache to read the data.

statement: Adding the cache saves expensive database queries and the load on the database, because queries are now answered by the cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you are saving an expensive database query, the load on your database, because the queries are now answered by your cache.

statement: For a popular blog, repeatedly doing an expensive three-four table join on the database to get the blog data puts unnecessary load on the database, so the blog is cached in the centralized remote cache; the request then goes to the cache, which is much faster and cuts database load by a massive margin.
case_study: Get-a-blog request on the blogging app.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: doing that expensive three four table join on database to [unclear: "grid"] that blog data again and again puts unnecessary load on the database.

statement: The remote cache still costs a network IO, but reading a pre-computed result from the cache is much faster than going to the database, recomputing and sending it back.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: reading from the cache pre-computed is much faster than going to the database, recomputing it and sending it back

statement: Caching internals will be covered in depth later: a distributed/remote cache and key-value store will be built in weeks three to five, with extreme detail on eviction, LRU, LFU and so on; some of it also comes up the next day.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We'll build distributed cache, remote cache, key-value store, there we'll go into details of it, like third week, fourth week, fifth week

statement: Exercise for the next day's first 30 minutes: on this common architecture diagram, find all possible places you can use as a cache, with an example, what you cache there and what problem it solves; students who raise hands pitch one use case each.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: find possible places where you can use as a cache with an example.

statement: In the third or fourth cohort, about two years earlier, the same caching-places discussion led a participant working at Goldman Sachs to propose a new caching place to his manager; it was approved and gave a massive performance boost, a use case they had not thought of.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: that person worked at Goldman Sachs. He took that approach, proposed it to his manager. Manager approved it

statement: One caching place already covered is the centralized (application-level) cache that every API server talks to, which saves expensive DB calls/computation; CDN and load balancer are hints for other places to look.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDN might be one. Load balancer might be another. Think on those lines.

statement: Everything has a trade-off: when you use some place as a cache you gain something and lose something; the next day's discussion is trade-off based.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So when you use something, some place as a cache, you get something, you lose something.

statement: After the caching discussion, the next session covers the other four foundational components with the same example: concurrency, communication, scaling and delegation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll discuss on the other four components of foundational topics with the same example. So concurrency, communication, scaling, and delegation.

statement: A student who thought caches must be in RAM asked why expensive computation results cannot simply be pre-computed and stored in a database table; the teacher said that is a possible place too.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And then that is a possible place. That is a possible place.

statement: Always ask 'why not this, why just this?' instead of being obsessed with storing caches in RAM: what matters is that the business and products work and perform, however you do it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why are we, why the entire world is obsessed with just storing it in RAM?

statement: A student asked whether client-side local storage also counts as caching; the teacher deferred it to the next day's discussion of the different places you can cache.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: when we use local storage, so that is, that also comes in caching means to store something.

statement: Marking many records as soft-deleted grows the database size, so soft-deleted rows are periodically hard-deleted, for example once a day pick up all soft deletes and hard delete them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say once a day you pick up all the soft deletes and you do hard delete on it.

statement: Instead of hard deleting, soft-deleted items can be moved somewhere else; that is archival.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Or, or move it to somewhere else. Like that's archival.

statement: When a soft-deleted item can be moved to hard deletion is very subjective.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: For soft deletes, when can you move an item which is soft deleted to hard deleted? Because it's very subjective.

statement: Under GDPR's right to be forgotten, if a user files a ticket with Facebook asking to delete everything it has on them, Facebook has to hard delete everything the user ever created within one month.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Facebook has to do hard delete of it in one month's time.

statement: Right-to-be-forgotten deletion does not have to be immediate; the one-to-two month window gives breathing space for cases such as the user having harassed someone.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it's not that they have to do it immediately. Right? Facebook has that time. One month, two month time to delete all.
flags: unclear: "had a so immediately pull this company"

statement: PII is deleted immediately, but logs have everything, so there are hacks to recover data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So the PIIs would be deleted immediately, but there are hacks to, uh, recover something.

statement: Atlassian had a mega outage where data was deleted and it took them 14 days to recover it; that they could recover shows no company hard deletes all data ever created - they hard delete for compliance only from specific tracked places, while logs and snapshots still hold everything.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Atlassian has this mega outage where they deleted the data and it took them 14 days to recover, right?

statement: If you take daily database snapshots, nobody goes back and updates all historical snapshots when a user exercises the right to be forgotten; the data remains there, but the transactional system holds no trace of it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: will you go and update all of your snapshots? No one does that.

statement: These are compliance hacks; the legal team helps navigate compliance to maximize what you can keep.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: See, these are all hacks. Legal team helps you with this to navigate through this compliance part, to maximize what you can.

statement: The teacher built GDPR compliance himself: it took him two months to make the entire org GDPR compliant, implementing the infrastructure-level pieces.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It took me two months to make the entire [?org | asr: "or"] GDPR compliant on this.

statement: GDPR is the compliance regulation that lets a user exercise the right to be forgotten (e.g. ask Instagram to delete everything about them); the organization then has to hard delete all of that user's data, and GDPR enforces this on every single organization.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So GDPR enforces that on every single organization. Every single.

statement: Whether to compress data in a cache depends on a trade-off: decompression costs time, so compress only if what you cache is gigantic (e.g. massive text blobs) and the decompress-and-read time beats reading the larger data and paying for the extra memory.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Depends. Because then you are, then you would, then your trade-off comes in. Decompression. Decompression is a trade-off, right?

statement: The cache will not do compression for you since most caches are just key-value: the application must compress before storing and decompress after reading.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But then compression, cache will not do compression for you. You have to do it on the application.

statement: There are probably plugins for most caches that do compression, but the teacher is not sure of any and has never used one, never having found a genuine use case for storing massive data in a cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I think there would be plugins for most of the caches out there that does compression, but not sure of any.

statement: Compressing a small field such as an email ID gives no boost and actually loses performance on decompress, but compressing an entire blog body - say 10 KB stored as 1 KB - would be a huge benefit.
case_study: Caching a full blog body in the blogging app.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: compressing it and storing it in let's say one KB would be a huge benefit

statement: A student noted services like Instagram cache videos, video parts or images around the world; the teacher said CDNs distribute it and nothing stops you from compressing it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDN said they would be distributing it, but you can compress this.
flags: check: "CDN" may end the student's sentence

statement: Caches should never offer compression out of the box; it should be the application's responsibility, because compressing on the client side means transferring 1 KB over the network instead of 10 KB that ends up stored as 1 KB anyway.
detail: The teacher reasoned this out live ('now that I think of it'): saving memory in the cache while still shipping the uncompressed bytes over the network wastes bandwidth.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So, caches should never offer you compression out of the box. It should be your responsibility, logic that would do that.

statement: Application-side compression flow: compress on your end, send it, store it, receive it, decompress it and return it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So compress on your end, send it, [?store it | asr: "story"], receive it, decompress it and return.

statement: Keep asking questions: they surface use cases the teacher would otherwise find hard to cover; his answers come from experience when someone asks.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So keep asking questions, it just helps everyone, right?

statement: A student, cross-questioned in an interview, asked how to keep a highly available service when a cron job hard-deletes soft-deleted entries; the teacher said a cron job has nothing to do with availability.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Cron job has nothing to do with availability.

statement: Hard-deleting soft-deleted entries should cause no downtime in the main service; you do staggered deletions at a linear pace.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There would not be any downtime in your service when you're deleting, when you're just doing hard deletes, why would there be a downtime?

statement: The interviewer's concern about locking table entries while deleting is about strong consistency, not availability: you lock and delete rather than directly deleting so that stale reads of an already-deleted entry do not happen.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's not going down. That's just about being strongly consistent.

statement: Strong consistency will be covered next week (Saturday) in the databases session.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll talk about strong consistency next week, uh, next week, uh, Saturday, when we talk about databases.

statement: Comparing a Redis cache with a database table holding the same pre-computed results, from first principles: the application server holds persistent connections to both, so the connection cost cancels out.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: both have persistent connections, Redis also and your relational database also, so that is negated.

statement: Redis reads the value from memory, whereas the database goes to disk to read it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when it reads from memory, here it reads from the disk.

statement: For very small reads (say 10-15 bytes) memory is much faster than disk because disk is humongously slow for small reads; for large reads (say 1 KB) the difference is minimal - Redis is still a little faster, but not hugely.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this guy is humongously slow when you are reading small reads.

statement: A disk-based database stores data in a B+ tree, so a read needs a disk traversal of about log n reads depending on the number of rows, while an in-memory hash gets the value in one shot.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Your disk based databases stores it in terms of B plus tree.

statement: Storing in memory costs more and the amount you can store is limited by RAM; a database is limited by disk, so you get a larger cache on disk versus a smaller cache in memory.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The amount you can store is limited by the RAM and not by the disk.

statement: Choosing between a Redis cache and a DB table is subjective: weigh what and how much you read, how data is stored, how many IOs happen, the actual advantage and how much data you store; overall there is not much difference.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it's very subjective. So what you're reading, how much are you reading? How your data is stored? How many IOs would happen?

statement: RAM is more expensive than disk, and that is the biggest factor in this choice.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: RAM is more expensive than disk, so that is the biggest factor.

statement: With a managed Redis service, the cloud provider does all the management and charges its own pricing, so cost has to be considered.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: then the entire management is done by the cloud. So they have their own pricing and billings and whatnot.

statement: If pre-computed results are stored in the same database that serves your application, the database also spends time processing these reads, which affects existing requests.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the database will also spend time processing this, so existing requests will take an effect.

statement: The whole domain is filled with trade-offs; there is no one right answer to anything - even 2 plus 2 can be reformulated - so always be open to trade-offs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Our entire domain is filled with trade-offs. There is no one right answer to anything.

statement: If a cron job must hard delete many soft-deleted rows (e.g. 100,000) while traffic is high, you must not delete them in one shot: do staggered deletion spread across the day, like garbage collection - for example 10,000 rows every hour, or about 1,000 rows at a time - to minimize the impact.
detail: The teacher's numbers shifted as he spoke (one-hour job deleting 1,000 rows; half-hour job; 10,000 rows split across 10 hours, corrected to 10,000 rows every hour).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You cannot delete all 100,000 rows in one shot. Split it across your entire day.

statement: A follow-up noted that an hourly cron job also takes one or two connections from the connection pool, while not deleting lets data grow; the teacher answered that you gain some and lose some - you never win it all.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is nothing like you don't win it all. Never. You win something, you lose something.

statement: Soft delete conflicts with a uniqueness index (e.g. on email): if a user deletes their account and wants to create a new one with the same email, the soft-deleted row blocks it, so in this use case the row has to be hard deleted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So then there has to be hard in this use case. It has to be hard deleted.

statement: Setting a retention policy in the database instead of running a cron job still means someone does the deletion: a database thread does it, i.e. you offload the cron job to the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So then DB would be having thread that is doing it. So DB is doing the cron job for you, right?

statement: For regular-interval deletes, the approach that always works for DB performance is to offload it to the database and do it in a staggered way.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Offload it to database, do it in a staggered way. Yeah, always works.

statement: Comparing the database with the cache assumes the worst case, a disk read; in the best case the table is small enough that the database keeps it in RAM and there is no difference.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The best case is that the table is so small that it fits in the RAM and database is keeping it in the RAM.

statement: Indexing a field does not guarantee RAM reads: if there is not enough RAM to fit the index, the read goes to disk; always design for the worst case, a disk read.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you don't have enough RAM to fit in that index, then, okay, you always go for the worst case.

statement: If you work for Google and are bound to GCP, you are the vendor yourself and will never move out, so vendor lock-in is not a concern; likewise a company sure it will always stay on AWS need not worry about vendor lock-in.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: then you, then you, you yourself are the vendor. You would never be moving out, right?

statement: Wearing a manager's hat, another factor is talent: it is easier to hire people who know a widely used open-source technology than a proprietary vendor-only one, which may tempt a manager towards open source.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: is it easy for me to find talent who knows this particular technology that only this particular vendor offers versus an open source technology

statement: TigerGraph is a proprietary graph database while Neo4j is widely known: you would find hundreds of developers who know Neo4j but few who know TigerGraph.
detail: The teacher first started to cite Aerospike, then switched to TigerGraph.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I would find hundreds of developers who know Neo4j, but few who knows TigerGraph, right?

statement: Availability was left out of the DynamoDB vs Redis comparison by assuming it equal: with Redis your engineers must ensure availability, with DynamoDB AWS gives it, and availability is a property of engineers, not the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: availability is a property of engineers and not database.

statement: Showing 'last seen' was out of scope for the online/offline indicator (only green and gray); if you need it, you cannot delete the rows - keep them, and the last heartbeat received is the last-seen time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But if you need that, then you cannot delete the rows. Then you keep the rows.

statement: How Redis automatically expires keys (TTL implementation) will be discussed in week three when designing a cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We'll discuss this in third week. When we design cache, we'll have this discussion on this.

statement: Database indexes are permanently stored on disk, always; the teacher's YouTube video on how indexes make database reads faster explains it and will be in next week's pre-reads.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Permanent is always [?disk | asr: "this"], always, always, always, always.

statement: Soft delete and archival are not the same thing: soft delete allows you to archive, because with hard delete there is no time to archive.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, soft delete allows you to archive.

statement: Soft delete gives time to archive later (e.g. after a day): collect all soft-deleted rows, put them elsewhere, then hard delete; hard deleting and immediately copying each row to S3 would be slow.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because imagine you are doing hard delete and immediately copying it on S3. How slow would that be?

statement: A student asked why the online/offline solution started directly with Redis or DynamoDB as the main database rather than a database plus a cache; the teacher said Redis can be the primary database - why not.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I use Redis as a [unclear: "primary DVO worker"]. Why not?

statement: Whether to use a primary database with Redis on top or just Redis depends on the guarantees your system needs to provide.
detail: A student framed it as a trade-off on whether the data must be persisted; the teacher said the student had all the points.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now, depending on the guarantees that your system would need to provide, you pick one over the other.

statement: Using Redis as the primary DB for the online/offline indicator is fine: configure AOF-based persistence to get on-disk persistence with zero data loss, keep the speed, and the data is small enough (only 8 GB) to fit in RAM.
case_study: Online/offline indicator: 8 GB of status data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I can just configure [?AOF | asr: "AI"] based persistence on Redis and I'll get [?on-disk | asr: "on this"] persistence for that.

statement: Drop hard stereotypes like 'DynamoDB is only for this' or 'SQL is only for that'; what matters is knowing how to leverage a particular tech.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it just depends on how you know how to leverage a particular tech, that's all matters, right?

statement: Autoscaling under sudden surges is a property of engineering teams rather than the tool; the comparison assumed surge handling equal, but if considered, self-hosted Redis needs engineering expertise to manage, scale and react to surges, which counts against it versus DynamoDB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So that's a property of engineering teams rather than the tool itself, right?

statement: With a lean team you can offload everything to DynamoDB: you throw money at them and they become your extended engineering team.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You throw money at them, they become your extended engineering team.

statement: Avoiding DB-specific features: TTL was chosen because expiration was needed, so the database was picked for it (DynamoDB and Redis give it); you need some features (e.g. ACID) and would move only to a database giving similar features, or re-implement the feature, e.g. a cron job that does the same thing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If not, you always have an option to re-implement it. For example, writing a cron job that does that exact same thing.

statement: Draw a line on how far you abstract: drop the unrealistic concerns, focus on realistic ones and then design the system; otherwise you fall into a rabbit hole and end up writing your own database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Otherwise you'll drop the rabbit hole and eventually write your own database. Don't do that.

statement: If you leave DynamoDB you would not use DynamoDB Streams, but CDC tools give you the same: with MySQL, use Debezium to capture changes; either something managed provides it or you write a small service.
detail: A student's TTL-plus-streams archival proposal had been challenged by a senior engineer as Dynamo-only.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you're using MySQL, use Debezium to capture all this.

statement: Document the limitations of your design and the steps you would take if you ever had to migrate; being aware of your design's limitations is a good place to be.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: just being aware of the limitations of your design is a good place to be.

statement: Whether connection pools multiply when you scale the database from one to two depends on how you scale; write a hello-world with connection pooling against a local database today to see its configurations and limitations. Horizontal scaling of databases comes next week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Today, spend some time writing a hello world with connection, [?pooling | asr: "pulling"] local database, run it.

statement: Whether to show last seen (like WhatsApp) is a product call: if they want it, you cannot delete offline entries; there is nothing to optimize because storage is not a problem - 8 GB is peanuts.
case_study: Online/offline indicator, 8 GB of status data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You cannot, because storage is not a problem, right? It's just 8 GB of storage.

statement: Downside of connection pooling: with a database supporting at most 1,000 connections and a per-server pool with a minimum of 100, adding servers as traffic grows works until a massive spike makes you add 20 more and you exhaust the database's maximum connections.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You exhausted the maximum number of connections that could be made with the database.

statement: A misconfigured connection pool limits the number of API servers you can have: the maximum is a factor of the pool's minimum connections per server and the database's maximum connections, so blindly using connection pooling is not a good idea.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So by not configuring your connection pool properly, you can limit the number of API servers that you can have.

statement: If the pool may grow to as many connections as it wants, you cannot have many servers; and with a very high connection expiry (e.g. 10 minutes) one server hogs database connections, so new servers the load balancer routes users to cannot get connections - an outage for those users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: some other server is [?hogging | asr: "fogging"] up the database connections. Now what? Gone. You're having an outage, right?

statement: Grass is not always green: know how and where to tune and where it can break; think in multiple directions, document everything and go step by step through what could go wrong, then find a near-optimal solution and move on.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Life is filled with problems. Just find a near optimal solution and move on.

statement: Start conservatively: a connection pool's minimum is three to five connections, allowed to grow to a certain stage, maybe less than 50 or 100.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you start with three or five, not more than that, and you make it grow to a certain stage, maybe less than 50 or 100.

statement: The connection TTL (time after which a pooled connection is removed) must not be too small, nor too large, which leaves many unused connections; find the sweet spot for the use case - long-running queries need connections open longer, so a short TTL does not work.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If it's too large, then you are having unused, a large number of unused connections. So you need to find a sweet spot

statement: The most important metric for tuning a connection pool is the average SQL query completion time on your database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: one factor or one metric that you should track is average time for SQL query completion on your database workflow.

statement: If the average query time for a frequently used query goes up, the connection pool for that DB should be expanded.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Then if we have a very frequent use case for that, we should think about expanding our connection pool for that DB.
flags: check: "Correct." may be the teacher answering

statement: How a database server sustains more than 30,000 TCP connections was left for students to Google (Hussein Nasser's video, Stack Overflow answers, a hardware specification); the teacher will answer by week three if needed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So, Hussain Nasser has a great video on that. You'll find a couple of Stack Overflow answers on it.

statement: TTL in Redis was used because space was important; if space is not important you skip it and keep the entries, and the extra computation is not a concern because in-memory deletion is peanuts for Redis.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: much because it's in-memory deletion. It's peanuts for Redis.

statement: Trade-off intuition is built over the eight weeks: every system designed will discuss trade-offs for hours, and next week's brainstorming will not move forward without answers on why a decision is made and its trade-offs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll not move forward unless and until we have answers that why are we making a certain decision, what are the trade-offs for that

statement: Where to stop overthinking is covered in week six, day two, by looking at the same system from manager, product manager, senior engineer and junior engineer perspectives ('three hats').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll think from different perspectives, same system from a management perspective, from managers, from product managers perspective

statement: HTTP is designed to be stateless - one request, one response, deal done - but you can still keep a persistent HTTP connection via the keep-alive header.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: HTTP in itself is a stateless thing. Okay. Which means that it's one request. You send a request, you get a response, deal done

statement: HTTP/2 keeps persistent connections; WebSocket is not HTTP but also keeps a persistent connection; no rule says you must always terminate the connection.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: HTTP/2 keeps the persistent connections. WebSocket keeps up. WebSocket is not HTTP, but it keeps the persistent connection.

statement: Normally the client sends a request, the server responds and terminates the connection; with the keep-alive header the web server does not terminate it, and if neither side terminates, the connection stays open.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Which is what this keep-alive header that you pass in to keep the connection open does for you.

statement: Think of HTTP as stateless - it simplifies design; when you need state, better options exist such as WebSockets or MQTT.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: understand that HTTP, think of it as a stateless. It would simplify your design much

statement: A future system will use HTTP/2 to keep connections stateful; this is covered in week five, day two.
